Correct Answer(s): Add a deployment gate

Add a deployment gate is the CORRECT answer because a gate is configured as part of a release process to set caps or baselines for deployments to succeed. Gate in a pipeline helps to check the code against a set of rules and only passes a release if the code matches the set baseline of configured rules(in our case the releases must comply with the Azure Policy rules assigned to a Sub1 Azure subscription). If the code does not pass the gate check, the release fails.
Gates allow automatic collection of health signals from different services (Azure policies at the subscription scope in our case) and then promote the release when all the signals are successful (required status checks) at the same time or stop the deployment on timeout.
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops

Modify the Deployment queue settings is the INCORRECT answer because this setting defines the behaviour of the deployment queues when multiple releases are queued for deployment.

Configure a deployment trigger is an INCORRECT answer because this setting is used when we want to set up a trigger (manual, after a stage or after a build) to kick start some specific deployment stage.

3. Import a Desired State Configuration (DSC) configuration into the Azure Automation account.

explanation_html:

We use Azure automation state configuration service to achieve the desired functionality and leverage automation to reduce manual intervention.

To onboard the Web server virtual machines with IIS on Azure automation state configuration we will perform the following steps in order:
1. As a prerequisite, we need an Azure automation account to automate the whole workflow process
2. Once we have the azure automation account, we need to create a PowerShell DSC script and import that DSC configuration script into the Azure automation account

question_html:
You have a build pipeline in Azure pipelines that occasionally fails.
You discover that a test measuring the response time of an API endpoint causes the failures.
You need to prevent the build pipeline from failing due to the test.
Which two actions should you perform?

options.text: Manually mark the test as flaky
Set Flaky test detection to Off.
Clear Flaky tests included in test pass percentage.

explanation_html:
Correct Answer(s):  Manually mark the test as flaky and Clear Flaky tests included in test pass percentage

Clear Flaky tests included in the test pass percentage and Manually mark the test as flaky are the two actions that well perform to prevent the build pipeline from failing due to flaky tests.
Flaky tests inhibit a developers ability to work productively and troubleshoot the real bugs because of the build pipeline failures due to some flaky tests. These tests provide different outcomes of a pass or fail, even when there are no changes done in the source code or the execution environment.
Flaky test management capabilities of azure pipelines help to manage these tests more efficiently by reducing the chances of build failure due to them.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/flaky-test-management?view=azure-devops

Set Flaky test detection to Off is an INCORRECT choice because this will disable the auto-detection feature of azure pipelines for detecting flaky tests. This is the exact opposite of what is required and that is why we rule this option out.

Enable test slicing is an INCORRECT answer because this option will allow the pipelines to run tests(Eg: Visual studio test task in pipelines) in parallel on multiple agents. This will not help us in managing the flaky tests.
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/parallel-testing-vstest?view=azure-devops

Enable Test Impact Analysis (TIA) is an INCORRECT answer because this feature is used for incremental validation by automatic test selection from the Visual Studio test task in pipelines. It doesnt help in dealing with the flaky tests and that is why we rule this option out.
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/test-impact-analysis?view=azure-devops

question_html:
You have an Azure Resource Manager template that deploys a multi-tier application.
You need to prevent the user who performs a deployment from viewing the account credentials and connection strings used by the application.
What should you use?

options.text: an Azure Resource Manager parameter file

explanation_html:
Correct Answer(s): Azure Key Vault

Azure Key Vault is the CORRECT answer because we need to prevent the user who performs a deployment using azure resource manager templates from viewing the account credentials and connection strings used by the application. 
Azure Key Vault is a secure cloud storage place for secrets, certificates, keys, or any credentials. We can use the ARM template parameters file to refer to the values of key vault entities from the key vault securely without the credentials being exposed anywhere in the process. Please see the below snippet for an idea on how to refer to key vault secret from an ARM template parameters file:

“adminPassword”: {
    “reference”: {
        “keyVault”: {
        “id”: “/subscriptions//resourceGroups/mykeyvaultdeploymentrg/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/”
        },
        “secretName”: “vmAdminPassword”
    }
},

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/key-vault-parameter?tabs=azure-cli
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/template-tutorial-use-key-vault

an Azure Resource Manager parameter file is an INCORRECT answer because the parameters file alone cannot fulfill our requirement. Moreover, using a parameters file is just a way of referencing a particular secret and key vault. The main thing is the key vault which holds a secret value.

A Web.config file is an INCORRECT answer because this file is responsible for holding the configuration settings data for a web application and is not helpful in this case to keep the secrets safe.

An appsettings.json file is an INCORRECT answer because this file holds the application-specific configuration data like database connections strings, any application scope global variables, etc.

An Azure storage table is an INCORRECT answer because this is a storage service for storing NoSQL data and has nothing to do with passing the credentials securely for an ARM template deployment.

question_html:
You have an Azure DevOps project that contains a build pipeline. The build pipeline uses approximately 50 open‑source libraries. You need to ensure that the project can be scanned for known security vulnerabilities in the open‑source libraries. What should you choose for Dropdown1?

What should you choose for Dropdown1?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option A. A build task

  • Correct because vulnerability scanning of open‑source libraries should be integrated into the build pipeline.
  • Build tasks such as WhiteSource Bolt, GitHub Advanced Security, or other security scanning extensions can automatically check dependencies during the build.
  • This ensures that vulnerabilities are detected early in the CI/CD process, aligning with DevSecOps best practices.

Incorrect

Option B. A deployment task

  • Incorrect because deployment tasks occur after the build and release stages.
  • Vulnerability scanning must happen before deployment, not after, to prevent insecure code from being released.

Option C. An artifacts repository

  • Incorrect because an artifacts repository stores build outputs (packages, binaries, etc.).
  • While repositories can enforce retention or versioning policies, they do not perform vulnerability scanning themselves.

question_html:
You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso, an Azure DevOps project named Project1, an Azure subscription named Sub1, and an Azure key vault named vault1.
You need to ensure that you can reference the values of the secrets stored in vault1 in all the pipelines of Project1. The solution must prevent the values from being stored in the pipelines.
What should you do?

options.text: Create a variable group in Project1.
Add a secure file to Project1.
Modify the security settings of the pipelines.
Configure the security policy of Contoso.

explanation_html:
Correct Answer(s): Create a variable group in Project1

Create a variable group in Project1 is the CORRECT answer because we want to use the values of some secrets (credentials) for all the pipelines of Project1, stored in a key vault in Azure. We use the variable groups from the library tab of an azure DevOps project and link a particular group to an azure key vault for synchronizing the secrets for use in all the pipelines of a particular project. We also get an option to select which secrets we want to synchronize with the Azure DevOps project, out of all the secrets that are protected inside the key vault.
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/variable-groups

Add a secure file to Project1 is an INCORRECT answer because secure files in a library are used to store certificates for different purposes like signing certificates, SSH certs, etc. However, they dont help in fetching secrets from a key vault to make them available for all pipelines to use.

Modify the security settings of the pipelines is an INCORRECT answer because by doing this we will be able to change the access level security for all of our pipelines. However, they arent helpful in referencing the values of the secrets stored in a key vault.

Configure the security policy of Contoso is an INCORRECT answer because this will not help us in referencing the values of the secrets stored in a key vault as Organization settings dont have such an option. Moreover, we want to use secrets from a key vault to be used in pipelines of a single project, not the whole organization.

What should you do?

options.text: Add a Docker Compose task to the build pipelines.
Change the self-hosted agent to use Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8.

explanation_html:
Correct Answer(s): Create two container jobs 

Create two container jobs is the CORRECT answer because we have a requirement to minimize the possibility of two build pipelines conflicting with each other while keeping the infrastructure costs to a bare minimum.
A container job in azure YAML pipelines, helps us run the builds inside a container on top of the operating system of the host machine (Windows Server 2019-based self-hosted agent). This gives us more control over the dependencies for every build and helps in reducing the possibility of conflict between two build pipelines. We can isolate resources/dependencies for different builds while using the same infrastructure by leveraging virtual environments(containers) for multiple builds.
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/container-phases?view=azure-devops
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/phases?view=azure-devops&tabs=yaml

Add another self-hosted agent is an INCORRECT answer because this will not minimize infrastructure costs, but instead increase it.

Change the self-hosted agent to use Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 is an INCORRECT answer because changing the operating system for the self-hosted machine will not help to isolate the dependencies and manage build conflicts.

Add a Docker Compose task to the build pipelines is an INCORRECT answer because Docker Compose helps us to faster deploy multiple container applications by using just one command to build the whole environment.

question_html:
Your team is currently using Azure Devops to manage a production-based environment. The team now wants to use Azure Devops to deploy Azure virtual machines to a staging environment. Below are the key requirements
Ensure the cost of hosting Azure resources is minimized
Provide the ability to automatically provision virtual machines
Use a custom Azure Resource Manager template to provision the virtual machines
Which of the following would you use as the implementation step for this requirement?

options.text: A. In Azure Devops , create new tasks in the release pipeline to deploy the new virtual machines
B. Run powershell commands in Azure Cloud shell to create and delete virtual machines
C. Run Azure CLI commands in Azure Cloud shell to create and delete virtual machines
D. Make use of the Azure DevTest Labs extension for Azure Devops

explanation_html:
Correct

Option D. Make use of the Azure DevTest Labs extension for Azure DevOps

  • Azure DevTest Labs is specifically designed to minimize costs by automatically managing VM lifecycles (auto‑shutdown, quotas, reusable templates).
  • It integrates with Azure DevOps pipelines, allowing automated provisioning of VMs using custom ARM templates.
  • This directly satisfies all three requirements: cost control, automation, and template‑based provisioning.

Incorrect

Option A. In Azure DevOps, create new tasks in the release pipeline to deploy the new virtual machines

  • While pipelines can deploy resources, this approach does not inherently minimize costs or provide VM lifecycle management.
  • It lacks the cost‑optimization features of DevTest Labs.

Option B. Run PowerShell commands in Azure Cloud Shell to create and delete virtual machines

  • This is a manual approach, not integrated with DevOps pipelines.
  • It does not provide automated provisioning or cost management.

Option C. Run Azure CLI commands in Azure Cloud Shell to create and delete virtual machines

  • Similar to PowerShell, this is manual and not aligned with DevOps automation.
  • It does not address cost minimization or reusable ARM template deployment in a controlled DevOps workflow.

Correct

Option A. A gate

  • Correct because gates in Azure Pipelines are used to enforce conditions or checks before a stage runs.
  • In this case, a gate can be configured to ensure that the VM meets the required SKU size before deployment proceeds.
  • Gates are ideal for validating external resources or compliance requirements before continuing with the pipeline.

Incorrect

Option B. A trigger

  • Incorrect because triggers define when a pipeline runs (e.g., on code push or schedule).
  • They do not enforce resource validation or SKU checks.

Option C. An agent

  • Incorrect because agents are the compute resources that run pipeline jobs.
  • While necessary for execution, they do not enforce VM SKU validation.

Option D. A package

  • Incorrect because packages are artifacts (like NuGet, npm, or container images) produced or consumed in pipelines.
  • They are unrelated to enforcing VM SKU requirements.

question_html: A company is currently developing a number of applications in their on‑premise environment. They want to make use of services in Azure by creating a hybrid connection. This needs to be a dedicated connection which provides high bandwidth. Which of the following would you consider for this purpose?
explanation_html:
Correct

  • Option D. ExpressRoute
    • Correct because Azure ExpressRoute provides a dedicated, private connection between on‑premises infrastructure and Azure.
    • It offers high bandwidth, low latency, and reliability, making it ideal for hybrid scenarios where enterprises need secure and consistent connectivity.
    • Unlike VPNs, ExpressRoute does not traverse the public internet, ensuring better performance and security.

Incorrect

  • Option A. Virtual Private Gateway
    • Incorrect because this is an AWS concept, not Azure. Azure uses VPN Gateway, but that is internet‑based and not dedicated high‑bandwidth like ExpressRoute.
  • Option B. Virtual Private Connection
    • Incorrect because this is not an Azure service. It is a generic term and does not represent the dedicated hybrid connectivity solution required here.
  • Option C. Virtual Network Peering
    • Incorrect because VNet Peering connects Azure VNets to each other, not on‑premises to Azure. It is useful for intra‑Azure communication but does not solve hybrid connectivity needs.

A company is planning on using Azure DevOps services for their build and release processes. They have a set of .Net applications that need to be incorporated into a build pipeline. Which of the following would be a task that would ideally go into Task2?

Correct

Option D. VSBuild Task

  • Correct because the first step in the build pipeline is to actually compile the .NET application using the VSBuild task.
  • SonarQube tasks (Prepare, Analyze, Publish) are integrated around the build, but the build itself must occur first to generate the binaries and code artifacts that SonarQube will analyze.
  • Therefore, Task1 in the YAML pipeline should be the VSBuild Task.

Incorrect

Option A. SonarQube Publish Task

  • Incorrect because publishing results is the final step, after analysis has been completed. It cannot be the first task.

Option B. SonarQube Prepare Task

  • Incorrect because preparation of SonarQube configuration happens before analysis, but it is not the first task in the pipeline. The build must occur first to produce code artifacts.

Option C. SonarQube Analyze Task

  • Incorrect because analysis runs after the build. It requires both preparation and compilation to be completed first.

Question
You need to configure a cloud service to store the secrets required by the mobile applications to call the share pricing service.
What should you include in the solution for Required secrets?
explanation_html:
Correct:

  • D. Username and password: The case study explicitly states that the share pricing service “will only support basic authentication over HTTPS.” Basic authentication, by definition, uses a username and password. Therefore, the required secrets to be stored for this service are the username and password.

Incorrect:

  • A. Certificate: While certificates are used for secure authentication, the case study specifically mentions “basic authentication,” which does not use certificates in the same way. Certificates would be used for client-side authentication or server-side identity verification, which is not what basic authentication requires.
  • B. Personal access token: Personal access tokens (PATs) are used for authentication with services like Azure DevOps or GitHub, providing a more secure alternative to a password. The case study, however, specifies the use of “basic authentication” for the share pricing service, which is not synonymous with using a PAT.
  • C. Shared Access Authorization token: Shared Access Signature (SAS) tokens are used to delegate access to Azure Storage resources. This is not the type of authentication specified for the share pricing service, which is a custom service using basic authentication.

question_html:
A team is currently working on a Java based project in an Azure Devops environment. A solution needs to be recommended to improve the quality of code within the Devops project.
Which of the following would you recommend?

options.text: For a Maven build task, enable CheckStyle
For a Maven build task, enable PMD
For a Gradle build task, enable CheckStyle
For an ANT build task, enable FindBugs

explanation_html:
Correct:

  • B. For a Maven build task, enable PMD: PMD is a static analysis tool for the Java language. It is commonly integrated with build automation tools like Maven to find common programming flaws, detect design issues, and check for code quality. By enabling PMD in the Maven build task, the team can automatically check their code for quality issues as part of the build pipeline, which is a standard practice for improving code quality in a DevOps environment.

Incorrect:

  • A. For a Maven build task, enable CheckStyle: CheckStyle is a tool for static code analysis that checks Java source code against a set of formatting and coding standards. While it is useful for enforcing consistency, it focuses primarily on code style rather than detecting deeper code quality issues, bugs, or potential vulnerabilities like PMD. Therefore, PMD is a more direct and comprehensive recommendation for “improving the quality of code.”
  • C. For a Gradle build task, enable CheckStyle: While CheckStyle can be used with Gradle, the question states the team is working on a Java-based project in an Azure DevOps environment, and a common solution is needed. While Gradle is a valid build tool, Maven is also extremely popular. More importantly, using CheckStyle alone focuses on style and not the broader quality issues that PMD addresses.
  • D. For an ANT build task, enable FindBugs: FindBugs is a static analysis tool that can be used with ANT. However, FindBugs has been superseded by a more actively maintained fork called SpotBugs. Both FindBugs and SpotBugs are excellent tools for finding bugs. However, PMD (and SonarQube, which often includes PMD and other tools) is a more comprehensive and widely recommended solution for improving overall code quality, as it looks beyond just potential bugs to include issues with code design and complexity. For a general recommendation to improve code quality, PMD is a more encompassing solution than just a bug finder.

Question
You need to configure a cloud service to store the secrets required by the mobile applications to call the share pricing service.
What should you include in the solution for Storage location?
explanation_html:
Correct:

  • B. Azure Key Vault: Azure Key Vault is the correct choice for storing secrets, such as the basic authentication credentials required by the mobile applications to call the share pricing service. It is a secure and centralized cloud service designed specifically for managing and protecting cryptographic keys, certificates, and secrets. This aligns with the principle of least privilege and provides a secure way to handle sensitive information without embedding it directly in the application code.

Incorrect:

  • A. Azure Data Lake: Azure Data Lake is a large-scale data repository for big data analytics. It is not designed for storing and managing application secrets. Using it for this purpose would be inappropriate and would not provide the necessary security features like access control and rotation of secrets.
  • C. Azure Storage with HTTP access: Azure Storage is a general-purpose storage solution. While you can store data in it, using it to store secrets with only HTTP access would be highly insecure. HTTP is not encrypted, meaning the secrets could be easily intercepted in transit.
  • D. Azure Storage with HTTPS access: While Azure Storage with HTTPS access is more secure than HTTP, it is still not the recommended solution for storing application secrets. Azure Key Vault is purpose-built for this task, offering a higher level of security, fine-grained access control, and other key management features that are not inherent to standard file storage. Using Azure Storage for secrets would not align with the best practices for security and the principle of least privilege.

A team is currently building and deploying an application using Azure services, including Azure DevOps. You need to advise on the right security tool to use during the following phases of the development lifecycle:

  • After a pull request
  • During the continuous integration phase
  • During the continuous delivery phase

Which of the following would you use for the continuous integration phase?
explanation_html:
Correct

  • Option B. Static Code Analysis
    • Static code analysis is the correct tool for the continuous integration (CI) phase.
    • It scans source code automatically during builds to detect security vulnerabilities, coding errors, and compliance issues before deployment.
    • This aligns with DevSecOps best practices, ensuring that insecure code does not progress further in the pipeline.

Incorrect

  • Option A. Penetration Testing
    • Penetration testing is typically performed after deployment or in later stages, not during CI.
    • It requires a running application to simulate attacks, so it is not suitable for the CI phase.
  • Option C. Threat Modeling
    • Threat modeling is a design‑time activity, usually performed before coding or early in the lifecycle.
    • It helps identify potential attack vectors but is not integrated into the CI pipeline.
  • Option D. Load Testing
    • Load testing evaluates performance and scalability under stress conditions.
    • It is part of continuous delivery or pre‑production testing, not CI security validation.

question_html:
Case Study:

Which of the following access level would you provide for the photonapp-developers group?
explanation_html:
Answer A
Since the development team only need the permission to install packages, the Reader access level should be sufficient enough. Below are the access levels given in the Microsoft documentation


Since this is the right access level, all other options are incorrect

A. Reader

  • The requirement states that the photonapp-developers group should be able to “install packages during development“. In Azure Artifacts, the Reader role has the permission to view and download packages from a feed. Installing packages typically involves downloading them, so the Reader role grants sufficient permission for this task while adhering to the principle of least privilege.

B. Collaborator

  • The Collaborator role in Azure Artifacts allows users to both consume (download) and publish (upload) packages to a feed. While this role would allow the developers to install packages, it also grants them the ability to publish packages, which is not explicitly required for their task. Providing the Collaborator role would violate the principle of least privilege.

C. Contributor

  • The Contributor role in Azure Artifacts also allows users to publish and consume packages. Similar to the Collaborator role, granting this level of access would give the developers more permissions than strictly necessary for installing packages, thus violating the principle of least privilege.

D. Owner

  • The Owner role in Azure Artifacts has full control over the feed, including the ability to create, delete, and manage permissions. This level of access is far beyond what the photonapp-developers group needs to simply install packages and significantly violates the principle of least privilege.

Ref: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/feeds/feed-permissions?view=azure-devops

Which of the following access level would you provide for the photonapp-admin group?

A. Reader

B. Collaborator

C. Contributor

  • The Contributor role in Azure Artifacts is similar to the Collaborator role, allowing users to contribute to feeds by publishing and consuming packages. It also does not include the ability to create feeds or manage feed permissions. This level of access is also insufficient for the photonapp-admin group.

question_html:
You manage an Azure web app that supports an e-commerce website.
You need to increase the logging level when the web app exceeds normal usage patterns. The solution must minimize administrative overhead.
Which two resources should you include in the solution?

options.text: an Azure Monitor alert that has a static threshold.
an Azure Monitor alert that has a dynamic threshold
an Azure Monitor alert that uses an action group that has an email action

explanation_html:
Correct:

  • B. an Azure Monitor alert that has a dynamic threshold: Dynamic thresholds in Azure Monitor are ideal for this scenario because they automatically adjust based on historical usage patterns of the web app. This minimizes administrative overhead as you don’t need to manually set or update a static threshold for a changing metric like web app usage. When the usage deviates from the normal pattern, the alert will be triggered.
  • C. an Azure Automation runbook: An Azure Automation runbook can be configured to execute a script or a series of commands in response to an Azure Monitor alert. In this case, the runbook can be used to programmatically increase the logging level of the web app when the dynamic threshold alert is triggered. This automates the process and meets the requirement to minimize administrative overhead.

Incorrect:

  • A. an Azure Monitor alert that has a static threshold: A static threshold would require you to define a fixed value for the web app usage. This is not ideal for “normal usage patterns” which can fluctuate. Using a static threshold would likely result in either false positives (alerting on a normal spike) or false negatives (not alerting when needed) and would require manual adjustments, which increases administrative overhead.
  • D. the Azure Monitor autoscale settings: Autoscale settings are used to automatically adjust the number of instances of a resource, such as a web app, based on demand. While useful for handling increased traffic, autoscale does not directly increase the logging level of the application. It is focused on performance and availability, not on changing diagnostic settings.
  • E. an Azure Monitor alert that uses an action group that has an email action: An action group with an email action is used to send a notification when an alert is triggered. While an email notification could be part of the solution to inform an administrator, it does not actually perform the required action of increasing the logging level. The email only alerts someone, who would then have to manually perform the task, which does not minimize administrative overhead.

question_html:
You are developing an iOS application by using Azure DevOps.
You need to test the application manually on 10 devices without releasing the application to the public.
Which two actions should you perform?

options.text: Deploy a certificate from an internal certification authority (CA) to each device.
Onboard the devices into Microsoft Intune.
Create a Microsoft Intune device compliance policy.
Distribute a new release of application.
Register the IDs of the devices in the Apple Developer portal.
Register the application in the iTunes store.

explanation_html:
To manually test an iOS application on 10 devices without releasing the application to the public, two key actions are required:

  1. Register the IDs of the devices in the Apple Developer portal: This allows the devices to install the application that is not yet publicly available on the App Store.
  2. Distribute a new release of the application: This creates a build of the application that can be installed on the registered devices for testing.

Here’s why the other options are not necessary for this scenario:

  • Deploy a certificate from an internal certification authority (CA) to each device: This might be required for some internal testing scenarios, but it’s not essential for installing a pre-release app on registered devices.
  • Onboard the devices into Microsoft Intune: Microsoft Intune is a mobile device management (MDM) tool that can be used to manage and secure devices. 1 While it can be helpful for enterprise deployments, it’s not strictly necessary for installing an app on a few devices for testing purposes.
  • Create a Microsoft Intune device compliance policy: Similar to Intune enrollment, creating a compliance policy is more for managing a large number of devices in an organization and not essential for this specific scenario.
  • Register the application in the iTunes store: Registering the application in the iTunes store would make it publicly available, which is the opposite of what we want for internal testing.

By following these two steps, you can distribute the pre-release app to the registered devices for manual testing without making it publicly available on the App Store.

question_html: A company wants to integrate the build of a set of applications into Azure DevOps. The applications are based on Erlang and Hack as the underlying programming language. You have to ensure that you can integrate these applications into Azure Build pipelines. Which of the following would you use in the build pipeline? You also have to minimize management overhead in the chosen solution.

options.text: A. Create an Azure DevOps self-hosted agent that would run on an Azure virtual machine as part of Azure stack.
C. Create an Azure DevOps self-hosted agent that would run on a Hyper-V machine
D. Create an Azure DevOps self-hosted agent that would run on Azure DevTest Labs

explanation_html:
Correct

Option B. Use a Microsoft-hosted agent

  • Correct because Microsoft-hosted agents in Azure DevOps provide preconfigured environments with common tools and SDKs.
  • They minimize management overhead since you don’t need to maintain infrastructure or manually configure build agents.
  • Even if Erlang and Hack are not natively supported, you can install required dependencies during the pipeline execution using scripts.
  • This is the most efficient and least management-intensive solution.

Incorrect

Option A. Create an Azure DevOps self-hosted agent that would run on an Azure virtual machine as part of Azure stack

  • Incorrect because while self-hosted agents allow customization, they require ongoing management and maintenance of the VM and agent software.
  • This increases overhead compared to Microsoft-hosted agents.

Option C. Create an Azure DevOps self-hosted agent that would run on a Hyper-V machine

  • Incorrect because this also requires provisioning and maintaining infrastructure.
  • Hyper-V adds complexity and does not minimize management overhead.

Option D. Create an Azure DevOps self-hosted agent that would run on Azure DevTest Labs

  • Incorrect because DevTest Labs is designed for testing environments, not production-grade CI/CD pipelines.
  • It introduces unnecessary overhead and is not the recommended approach for minimizing management.

Here’s why:

  • Therefore, keyvault is the necessary subcommand to specify that you are working with Key Vault secrets.

The complete command should look like this:

question_html:
You have 50 Node.js-based projects that you scan by using WhiteSource. Each project includes Package.json, Package-lock.json, and Npm-shrinkwrap.json files.
You need to minimize the number of libraries reports by WhiteSource to only the libraries that you explicitly reference.
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the scan to exclude devDependencies or filter reports
Configure the File System Agent plug-in.
Add a devDependencies section to Package.json.

explanation_html:
A. Configure the scan to exclude devDependencies or filter reports. (Correct)

The goal of “minimizing the number of libraries reported to only those explicitly referenced” refers to filtering out transitive dependencies or, more specifically, development-only dependencies that are not shipped with the production code.

  • Why it works: WhiteSource/Mend scans typically pick up every library found in the dependency tree. By configuring the npm.resolveDevDependencies setting to false in the WhiteSource configuration file (whitesource.config) or using the npm.ignoreNpmLsErrors flag, you prevent the tool from reporting libraries used only for testing or building (like Linters or Test Runners).

  • Alignment: This directly addresses the requirement to see only “explicitly referenced” (production) libraries.

B. Configure the File System Agent plug-in. (Incorrect)

The File System Agent (FSA) is the actual tool used to perform the scan. While you run the FSA, simply “configuring” the plug-in is too vague. The FSA is the how, but the specific logic to filter libraries must be done via the configuration parameters (as mentioned in Option A), not the existence of the agent itself.

C. Add a devDependencies section to Package.json. (Incorrect)

The scenario states that these are Node.js projects; they likely already have a devDependencies section if they are using standard modern workflows. Adding the section doesn’t hide anything from WhiteSource; in fact, without the exclusion filter mentioned in Option A, adding more libraries to a devDependencies section would actually increase the number of libraries reported.

D. Configure the Artifactory plug-in. (Incorrect)

The Artifactory plug-in is used when you are scanning artifacts stored in a JFrog Artifactory repository. While Artifactory is a valid component of a DevOps pipeline, it doesn’t solve the problem of filtering internal Node.js project dependencies defined in the local manifest files (package.json).

E. Delete Package-lock.json. (Incorrect)

This is a “destructive” and anti-pattern choice.

  • The Role of Lockfiles: package-lock.json and npm-shrinkwrap.json ensure deterministic builds by locking down the exact versions of all nested dependencies.

  • Consequence: Deleting them would make your builds unstable and would not necessarily reduce the WhiteSource report count, as WhiteSource would simply fall back to scanning the node_modules folder or the primary package.json, likely resulting in the same (or more fragmented) data.

Implementation:

When configuring Mend (WhiteSource) for Azure DevOps pipelines, you typically use a configuration file. To achieve the goal in this question, you would modify the configuration as follows:

// Example of a whitesource.config snippet
npm.resolveDevDependencies=false
npm.ignoreSourceFiles=true

question_html: A company is planning to deploy a server application to an Azure virtual machine. This will be running Windows Server 2019. The company also has an Azure Key Vault that stores secrets. You have to secure the key vault to secure API secrets for third-party integrations. Which of the following would you implement for this requirement? Choose three answers from the options given below.

options.text: Configure Role-based access control for the vault.
Change the application code to access the key vault.
Implement a Key Vault access policy.
Configure a system-assigned managed identity for the virtual machine.

explanation_html:
Here are the three best options to secure the key vault and API secrets for third-party integrations in this scenario:

  1. Configure Role-based Access Control (RBAC) for the vault:

    • This is fundamental for security. RBAC allows you to define fine-grained permissions for who can access the key vault and what actions they can perform.
    • You can create roles that grant specific permissions (read, write, delete, etc.) to different users, groups, or service principals. This ensures that only authorized entities can access the secrets they need.

  2. Implement a Key Vault Access Policy:

    • Key Vault Access Policies define which entities (users, applications, services) can access the key vault and what permissions they have.
    • For your virtual machine, you’ll create an access policy that grants it the necessary permissions to retrieve the API secrets.

  3. Configure a system-assigned managed identity for the virtual machine:

    • A system-assigned managed identity is an Azure identity that’s directly associated with your virtual machine.
    • This eliminates the need to manage and rotate credentials within the application code.
    • The virtual machine can use this identity to authenticate with the key vault and retrieve secrets securely.

Why the other options are less relevant:

  • Change the application code to access the key vault: While necessary to some extent, this is not the primary security measure. The focus should be on secure access control and authentication.
  • Configure Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC): DSC is excellent for managing and automating the configuration of your virtual machines. However, it’s not directly related to securing access to the key vault.

By implementing these three measures, you establish a robust security framework for accessing API secrets from the key vault within your Azure environment.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/tutorial-net-virtual-machine

question_html:
A company has the following Azure delivery pipeline in place


You need to add a pre-deployment gate to the Staging stage. It would be based on Azure Monitor alerts.
You need to ensure the following
Alerts have time to be generated so that they could be evaluated by the gate
You have to ensure that the gate fails if a maximum time period of 30 minutes is reached.
Which of the following would you configure for the gate to comply with the below requirement?
Alerts have time to be generated so that they could be evaluated by the gate

options.text: B. The time between re-evaluation of gates
C. Minimum duration for steady results after a successful gates evaluation
D. The timeout after which gates fail

explanation_html:
A. The delay before evaluation

Here’s why the other options are not the best fit:

  • B. The time between re-evaluation of gates: This option specifies the interval between subsequent evaluations of the gate. It won’t directly affect the initial evaluation after deployment.
  • C. Minimum duration for steady results after a successful gates evaluation: This option defines the minimum time the gate result (success) needs to persist before deployment proceeds. It’s not relevant to ensuring alerts have time to be generated.
  • D. The timeout after which gates fail: While this option sets the maximum time allowed for the gate to succeed (including waiting for alerts), it doesn’t directly address the time for alert generation.

Explanation:

  • Delay Before Evaluation: This setting introduces a waiting period before the first evaluation of the pre-deployment gate. This delay allows time for Azure Monitor alerts to be generated and propagate to the Azure DevOps pipeline. By setting an appropriate delay, you ensure the gate considers any active alerts before continuing with the deployment.

Additional Considerations:

  • The appropriate delay before evaluation depends on your environment and the expected time for alerts to be generated. You might need to adjust this value based on your specific needs.
  • It’s essential to monitor the gate’s performance and fine-tune the delay if necessary to achieve a balance between allowing time for alerts and avoiding unnecessary delays in the deployment pipeline.

By understanding these configurations, you can effectively implement pre-deployment gates based on Azure Monitor alerts in your Azure DevOps pipelines.

This can be accomplished with the setting ‘The delay before evaluation’.

This would give enough time for the alerts to be in a state that they communicate their status to the gates

The Microsoft documentation mentions the following on this setting

A DevOps team is planning on deploying a web application onto an Azure Web App service. In order to cater to testing of new release , they decide to make use of deployments slots in the Azure Web App service. They have an App service plan in place that is based on the Standard tier.
They have to create a script to perform the following steps
1. Create a web app and attach it to the App service plan
2. Create a deployment slot
3. Initiate a swap of the deployment slots
You have to complete the below script for this requirement
SLOT_1 -ResourceGroupName [resource group name] -Name [app name] -Location [location] -AppServicePlan [app service plan name]

SLOT_2 -ResourceGroupName [resource group name] -Name [app name] -Slot [deployment slot name] -AppServicePlan [app service plan name]

$ParametersObject = @{targetSlot = “[slot name  e.g. “production”]”}
SLOT_3 -ResourceGroupName [resource group name] -ResourceType Microsoft.Web/sites/slots -ResourceName [app name]/[slot name] -Action applySlotConfig -Parameters $ParametersObject -ApiVersion 2015-07-01
Which of the following would go into SLOT_3?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option D. Invoke-AzResourceAction This is the correct cmdlet for triggering a deployment slot swap programmatically. While there is a specific Switch-AzWebAppSlot cmdlet, in many advanced automation scripts or when using generic resource parameters as shown in the snippet ($ParametersObject), Invoke-AzResourceAction is used to call the specific “slot swap” action on the Azure Resource Manager (ARM) provider. It is highly versatile and used frequently in DevOps pipelines to perform actions that don’t have a simple “New” or “Set” verb.

Incorrect

Option A. New-AzWebAppSlot This cmdlet is used to fulfill Step 2 of the requirement (creating the deployment slot). However, it cannot be used to “initiate a swap.” Its sole purpose is the creation and configuration of a new slot (like “staging”) under an existing Web App.

Option B. New-AzResourceGroup This cmdlet creates a logical container for Azure resources. While it is often the first step in a deployment script, it does not interact with App Service features or deployment slots directly, making it irrelevant to the specific task of initiating a swap.

Option C. New-AzWebApp This cmdlet fulfills Step 1 of the requirement. It creates the primary Web App instance and links it to the App Service Plan. It defines the “Production” slot by default but does not have the capability to perform a swap operation between existing slots.

question_html:
A team is using Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates in their DevOps pipeline. The templates need to access secrets stored in Azure Key Vault. You must ensure that the ARM template can successfully access the secrets using the principle of least privilege.

Which of the following would you use to restrict access to the secrets in the Key Vault service?

explanation_html:
Correct

Option A. Key vault access policy

  • Correct because Key Vault access policies are the traditional way to grant fine‑grained permissions (like get, list, set) to specific identities for secrets, keys, and certificates.
  • This aligns with the principle of least privilege, as you can grant only the required actions to the service principal or managed identity used by the ARM template.
  • For exam purposes, this is the expected answer since ARM templates typically rely on access policies for Key Vault integration.

Incorrect

Option B. Key Vault advanced policy access

  • Incorrect because there is no such feature called “advanced policy access” in Azure Key Vault.
  • This option is a distractor.

Option C. Role based access control (RBAC)

  • Incorrect in this exam context. While modern Key Vaults can use Azure RBAC for data plane access, the exam question emphasizes restricting access for ARM templates.
  • The expected answer is access policies, not RBAC, because RBAC is broader and not the default mechanism for ARM template secret retrieval.

Option D. Azure policies

  • Incorrect because Azure Policy is used for governance and compliance (e.g., enforcing allowed VM SKUs or requiring tags).
  • It does not directly control access to Key Vault secrets.

question_html: A development team is currently responsible for creating custom Nuget packages. Azure Artifacts is being used to host these packages. These packages need to be made available to anonymous users outside of the organization. Which of the following could be done to implement this requirement and also ensure that the number of publication points are minimized?

options.text: A. Ensure a new feed is created for the package
B. Make the Nuget repository as public
C. Create a new feed URL for the package
D. Publish the package to Github

explanation_html:
B. Make the Nuget repository as public

Explanation:

  • Minimizing Publication Points: Making the entire Nuget repository public within Azure Artifacts is the most efficient way to minimize the number of publication points. You don’t need to create separate feeds or URLs for each package.

  • Anonymous Access: When the repository is public, anonymous users can access and download the packages without requiring any authentication.

Why other options are less suitable:

  • A. Ensure a new feed is created for the package: Creating a new feed for each package would significantly increase the number of publication points, making management more complex.
  • C. Create a new feed URL for the package: Similar to option A, creating a new URL for each package would increase the number of publication points and make it harder to manage.
  • D. Publish the package to Github: While Github can host NuGet packages, it might not be the most suitable solution if the primary package management and distribution strategy is already centered around Azure Artifacts.

In summary:

Making the Nuget repository public within Azure Artifacts is the most efficient and straightforward approach to make custom NuGet packages available to anonymous users while minimizing the number of publication points.

question_html:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals.

The lead developer at a company reports that adding new application features takes longer than expected due to a large accumulated technical debt.
You need to recommend changes to reduce the accumulated technical debt.

Solution: You recommend increasing the test coverage.

Does this meet the goal?
explanation_html:
No

Explanation:

While increasing test coverage is generally a good practice, it does not directly address the root cause of the problem: accumulated technical debt.

  • Technical Debt refers to shortcuts or suboptimal design choices made during development for faster delivery, but which ultimately lead to increased development time and maintenance costs in the long run.

How increasing test coverage might help, but not directly address the debt:

  • Improved code quality: More tests can help identify and prevent regressions caused by changes to existing code, which can be a symptom of technical debt (e.g., tightly coupled components).
  • Increased confidence in refactoring: With good test coverage, developers can refactor code (improve its structure and design) with more confidence, as the tests will help ensure that the refactoring does not break existing functionality. This can help reduce technical debt over time.

However, increasing test coverage alone won’t:

  • Automatically fix existing design flaws: It doesn’t address the underlying issues that led to the technical debt in the first place.
  • Prevent future technical debt: It doesn’t directly discourage developers from making short-term decisions that create technical debt in the future.

To truly reduce accumulated technical debt, you need to:

  • Identify and address the root causes: Analyze the codebase to pinpoint areas with high technical debt (e.g., tight coupling, code duplication, lack of modularity).
  • Refactor the code: Invest time in refactoring the code to improve its design, maintainability, and testability.
  • Implement code reviews: Encourage peer code reviews to identify and prevent the introduction of new technical debt.
  • Prioritize code quality: Emphasize the importance of writing clean, maintainable code from the start.
  • Regularly address technical debt: Allocate dedicated time for addressing technical debt on a regular basis, instead of letting it accumulate further.

In summary: While increasing test coverage is a valuable practice, it’s not the most effective solution for reducing accumulated technical debt. A more comprehensive approach that addresses the underlying causes and actively improves the codebase is required.

question_html:
You are building an ASP.NET core application.
You plan to create an application utilisation baseline by capturing telemetry data.
You need to add code to the application to capture the telemetry data. The solution must minimise the costs of storing the telemetry data.
Which two actions should you perform?

options.text: Add the <initialsamplingpercentage>90</initialsamplingpercentage> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.
Add the <maxtelemetryitemspersecond>5</maxtelemetryitemspersecond> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.
From the code of the application, enable adaptive sampling.
From the code of the application, disable adaptive sampling.
From the code of the application, add Azure Application Insights telemetry.

explanation_html:
Correct Answers
Option C (From the code of the application, enable adaptive sampling): Adaptive sampling dynamically adjusts telemetry volume based on application load, reducing data sent to Application Insights while preserving critical data for baseline creation.
Option E (From the code of the application, add Azure Application Insights telemetry): Adding the Application Insights SDK is required to capture any telemetry data from the ASP.NET Core application.

Incorrect
Option A (Add the <InitialSamplingPercentage>90</InitialSamplingPercentage> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file): High initial sampling (90%) increases data volume and storage costs, contradicting the cost minimization requirement.
Option B (Add the <MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond>5</MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file): Fixed-rate config sampling doesn’t adapt to load changes and uses deprecated .config file approach for ASP.NET Core.
Option D (From the code of the application, disable adaptive sampling): Disabling sampling sends all telemetry data, maximizing storage costs instead of minimizing them.

question_html:
You are configuring the settings of a new Git repository in Azure Repos.

You need to ensure that pull requests in a branch meet the following criteria before they are merged:
– Committed code must compile successfully.

Which policy type should you configure for the above requirement?
explanation_html:
• Build policy:
    In Azure Repos, a build policy is configured on a branch to require that a build pipeline runs successfully before a pull request can be completed. This means the committed code must compile, pass tests, etc., before merging. This matches perfectly the requirement that code must compile successfully.
  • Check-in policy:
    This term is from older version control systems like Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC). It applies to gated check-ins or pre-check-in validation, but not for Git pull requests in Azure Repos.
  • Status policy:
    This is used to require an external service to report a status (like quality checks, code scans) on the pull request. It does not necessarily require a build to run in Azure Pipelines.

question_html:
You are building an application that has the following assets:
Source code
Logs from automated tests and builds
Large and frequently updated binary assets
A common library used by multiple applications
Where should you store large and frequently updated binary assets?
explanation_html:
Correct 
Option D (Azure Storage): Large and frequently updated binary assets (like Docker images, installers, media files) belong in Azure Blob Storage due to its scalability, cost-effectiveness, and support for frequent updates without version control overhead.

Incorrect
Option A: Azure Artifacts stores packages (NuGet, npm, Maven) with versioning; unsuitable for large, frequently changing binaries.
Option B: Azure Pipelines builds and deploys code; doesn’t store assets long-term.
Option C: Azure Repos (Git/TFVC) handles source code and small files; poor performance for large binaries due to repository bloat.
Option E: Azure Test Plans manages testing; no asset storage capability.

question_html: Your team has an Azure DevOps project and an Azure subscription. The subscription contains an Azure SQL database named photonappdb. They want to create a release pipeline that uses the Azure SQL Database deployment task to update the database. Which of the following should they use as an artifact in the update process?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option B. A DACPAC file

  • Correct because the Azure SQL Database deployment task in Azure DevOps is designed to deploy a DACPAC (Data-tier Application Component Package) file.
  • A DACPAC contains the database schema and can be used to update or deploy changes to an existing Azure SQL Database.
  • This is the standard artifact for schema deployment in release pipelines.

Incorrect

Option A. A BACPAC file

  • Incorrect because a BACPAC file contains both schema and data, typically used for import/export or backup/restore scenarios.
  • It is not the artifact used in release pipelines for schema updates.

Option C. An LDF file

  • Incorrect because LDF files are transaction log files in SQL Server.
  • They are not used in Azure SQL Database deployments.

Option D. An MDF file

  • Incorrect because MDF files are primary database files in SQL Server.
  • Azure SQL Database does not use MDF/LDF files directly, and they cannot be deployed via DevOps pipelines.

question_html:
You are configuring the settings of a new Git repository in Azure Repos.

You need to ensure that pull requests in a branch meet the following criteria before they are merged:
– Pull requests must have a Quality Gate status of Passed in SonarCloud

Which policy type should you configure for the above requirement?
explanation_html:
C. A status policy

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

A. A build policy: While a build policy can be configured to run a CI/CD pipeline that includes SonarCloud analysis, the build policy itself doesn’t directly check the “Quality Gate status” reported by SonarCloud. A build policy primarily focuses on the success or failure of the build process (compilation, unit tests, etc.). You would integrate SonarCloud analysis within the build pipeline, and SonarCloud would publish its analysis results, including the Quality Gate status. However, the policy that enforces the “Passed” status before merging is not the build policy itself.

B. A check-in policy: Check-in policies were a feature in Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC), the centralized version control system that predates Git in Azure DevOps. Azure Repos uses Git, and check-in policies are not applicable to Git repositories. Therefore, this is not a valid policy type for the given requirement in Azure Repos.

Reasoning for the Correct Answer:

A status policy is the correct policy type to enforce the requirement of a “Passed” Quality Gate status from SonarCloud before a pull request can be merged in Azure Repos. Here’s why:

  • External Service Integration: Status policies allow you to integrate external services like SonarCloud with your pull request workflow.
  • Status Reporting: When SonarCloud analyzes the code in a pull request, it publishes a status to Azure DevOps indicating the outcome of its analysis, including the Quality Gate status (Passed, Failed, etc.).
  • Policy Enforcement: By configuring a status policy that requires the specific SonarCloud status to be “Passed,” you ensure that the pull request cannot be merged until SonarCloud reports a successful Quality Gate.

To implement this, you would typically:

  1. Configure SonarCloud integration with your Azure DevOps project and pipelines.
  2. Ensure that the build pipeline associated with the pull request runs SonarCloud analysis, which then publishes a status to the pull request.
  3. Configure a status policy on the target branch of the repository, specifying that the status reported by SonarCloud (or a specific check within SonarCloud’s status) must be “Passed” for the merge to be allowed.

question_html:
You are integrating Azure Pipelines and Microsoft Teams.
You install the Azure Pipelines app in Microsoft Teams.
You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso that contains a project name Project1.
You subscribe to Project1 in Microsoft Teams.
You need to ensure that you only receive events about failed builds in Microsoft Teams.
What should you do first?

options.text: From Microsoft Teams, run @azure pipelines subscribe https://dev.azure.com/ Contoso /Project1.
?From Azure Pipelines, add a Publish Build Artifacts task to Project1.
?From Azure Pipelines, enable continuous integration for Project1.

explanation_html:
From Microsoft Teams, run @azure pipelines subscriptions.

Here’s why:

  • List Existing Subscriptions: This command provides a list of all existing subscriptions for Azure Pipelines notifications in your Microsoft Teams channel. It allows you to see which pipelines you’re currently subscribed to and their configurations.
  • Identify Current Settings: By viewing the existing subscriptions, you can check if there’s already a subscription for Project1 and what events it triggers notifications for (e.g., all builds, successful builds, failed builds).
  • Plan for Filtering: Knowing the existing setup helps you determine the next steps. You might need to remove an existing subscription for all events or modify it to filter for failed builds only.

Running @azure pipelines subscribe is the most efficient way to gather information before configuring notifications for failed builds in Microsoft Teams.

Here’s what the other options are not the best choices:

  • @azure pipelines subscribe https://dev.azure.com/Contoso/Project1: This command subscribes to all events for Project1 by default. While it creates a subscription, it doesn’t address the need to filter for failed builds only.
  • Add Publish Build Artifacts Task: This task is used to publish build artifacts during the pipeline execution. It doesn’t directly affect notifications in Microsoft Teams.
  • Enable Continuous Integration: While enabling continuous integration might lead to more frequent builds, it doesn’t control the type of notifications received in Microsoft Teams.

question_html: Your company has a private project in Azure DevOps. You have to ensure that a project manager can create custom work item queries that can be used to report on the projects progress. The solution must use the principle of least privilege. To which security group must you add the project manager to?
explanation_html:
C. Contributors Adding the project manager to the Contributors security group provides the necessary permissions to create and save their own work item queries within the project. This aligns with the principle of least privilege, as it grants the specific ability needed without providing broader administrative rights.

A. Project Collection Administrators The Project Collection Administrators group has broad administrative control over the entire Azure DevOps organization. Granting this level of access to a project manager just to create work item queries violates the principle of least privilege. They would have far more permissions than required.

B. Readers The Readers security group has view-only access to the project. Members of this group cannot create or save work items or queries. Therefore, adding the project manager to this group would not allow them to fulfill the requirement.

D. Project Administrators The Project Administrators group has administrative control at the project level, including managing teams, areas, iterations, and project-level permissions. While they can create and share queries, granting this level of access solely for creating personal queries exceeds the principle of least privilege. The Contributors group provides sufficient permissions for this specific task.

Answer – C

To provide the privilege to create custom work item queries, you can add the user as part of the Project Collection Administrators group. This would allow you to create or edit a shared query.

For more information on query permissions, you can refer to the below link-

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/permissions?view=azure-devops&tabs=preview-page#project-level-groups

question_html:
Your team currently develops applications that are built around docker containers. You are planning on pushing the images and storing them in Azure container registry. Several application environments in Azure would then pull these images and run them as containers.
You have to ensure service principals are used to access the Azure container registry. You have to ensure the credentials for the service principal are stored in an existing Azure key vault instance.
You have to complete the below Azure CLI command to implement this requirement
SLOT_1 \
–vault-name $AKV_NAME \
–name $ACR_NAME-pull-pwd \
–value $(SLOT_2 \
–name $ACR_NAME-pull \
–scopes $(az acr show –name $ACR_NAME –query id –output tsv) \
–role acrpull \
–query password \
–output tsv)
Which of the following would go into SLOT_1?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option B. az keyvault secret set

  • To store credentials in Azure Key Vault, you must use the az keyvault secret set command.
  • This command creates or updates a secret in the specified Key Vault.
  • In this case, it stores the service principal password generated in SLOT_2.

Incorrect

  • The correct syntax requires az keyvault secret set.
  • Therefore, this option is invalid.

Option C. az ad sp create-for-rbac

  • This command is used to create a service principal with role assignments.
  • It is relevant for SLOT_2 (where the service principal is created and password retrieved), not SLOT_1.

question_html:
You use GitHub Enterprise Server as a source code repository
You create an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso.
In the Contoso organization, you create a project named Project1.
You need to link github.com commits, pull requests, and issues to the work items of Project1. The solution must use OAuth-based authentication.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence?

ACTIONS
1. From Project Settings in Azure DevOps, create a service hook subscription.
2. From Organisation settings in Azure DevOps, connect to Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
3. From Organisation settings in Azure DevOps, add an OAuth configuration.
4. From Developer settings in GitHub Enterprise Server, generate a private key.
5. From Developer settings in GitHub Enterprise Server, register a new OAuth app.
6. From Project Settings in Azure DevOps, add a GitHub connection.
explanation_html:
Correct:

The correct sequence of actions is 5, 3, 6.

  1. 5. From Developer settings in GitHub Enterprise Server, register a new OAuth app.
    • To use OAuth for connecting GitHub Enterprise Server with Azure DevOps, you must first register Azure DevOps as an OAuth application within your GitHub Enterprise Server instance. This step provides Azure DevOps with the necessary Client ID and Client Secret to initiate OAuth communication.
  2. 3. From Organization settings in Azure DevOps, add an OAuth configuration.
    • After registering the OAuth app in GitHub, you take the Client ID and Client Secret and configure them in your Azure DevOps organization settings. This step tells Azure DevOps how to authenticate with your GitHub Enterprise Server instance using the OAuth app you just created.
  3. 6. From Project Settings in Azure DevOps, add a GitHub connection.
    • Once the OAuth configuration is set up at the organization level, you can then add a GitHub connection at the project level (Project1). This connection uses the pre-configured OAuth settings to link your GitHub Enterprise Server repository to Project1, enabling the linking of commits, pull requests, and issues to Azure DevOps work items.

Incorrect:

  • 1. From Project Settings in Azure DevOps, create a service hook subscription.
    • Service hooks are used to integrate Azure DevOps with external services (like Jenkins, Slack, etc.) by notifying them of events. While useful for broader integrations, it’s not the primary mechanism for establishing the initial OAuth-based connection between GitHub Enterprise Server and Azure DevOps for linking work items. The GitHub connection itself handles the necessary event subscriptions for linking.
  • 2. From Organization settings in Azure DevOps, connect to Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
    • Connecting Azure DevOps to Azure AD is crucial for user authentication, authorization, and identity management within Azure DevOps itself. However, it’s not directly related to establishing an OAuth connection with an external Git provider like GitHub Enterprise Server. That external connection uses its own OAuth mechanism.
  • 4. From Developer settings in GitHub Enterprise Server, generate a private key.
    • Generating a private key in GitHub Developer settings is typically associated with GitHub Apps or SSH authentication, not the standard OAuth flow for integrating with Azure DevOps as described for linking commits/PRs/issues. While GitHub Apps offer a more granular permission model and might use private keys for authentication, the question specifically asks for “OAuth-based authentication,” which primarily involves registering an OAuth app and using its Client ID/Secret.

Correct 
option B. Git

Git is the recommended modern distributed version control system in Azure Repos for most teams. It supports branching, merging, and offline work – ideal for contemporary DevOps practices and cross-platform development.

Incorrect 
option A. Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC)
Centralized system requiring server connectivity for most operations. Better for legacy .NET Framework projects with large binary files, but Microsoft recommends Git for new projects.

question_html:
You use Azure Pipelines to manage project builds and deployments.
You plan to use Azure Pipelines for Microsoft Teams to notify the legal team when a new build is ready for release.
You need to configure the Organization Settings in Azure DevOps to support Azure Pipelines for Microsoft Teams.
What should you turn on?

options.text: Azure Active Directory Conditional Access Policy Validation

explanation_html:
Correct:

A. Third-party application access via OAuth

This is the correct option. The Azure Pipelines integration with Microsoft Teams is considered a third-party application accessing Azure DevOps services. OAuth (Open Authorization) is the standard, secure protocol used to grant third-party applications limited access to user accounts on an HTTP service, without giving them passwords. For the Azure Pipelines bot to authenticate with Azure DevOps and send notifications to Microsoft Teams, it requires this access method to be enabled at the organization level.

Incorrect:

B. Alternate authentication credentials

This option is incorrect. Alternate authentication credentials (like personal access tokens – PATs, or SSH keys for Git) are typically used for programmatic access by scripts or individual developers, not for a direct, service-to-service integration like Azure Pipelines for Microsoft Teams. OAuth is the designed method for this type of integration.

C. Azure Active Directory Conditional Access Policy Validation

This option is incorrect. Azure Active Directory Conditional Access policies are used to enforce security requirements (like multi-factor authentication, trusted locations) when users or applications try to access Azure AD-protected resources. While important for overall security, enabling or disabling this setting does not directly control the ability of the Azure Pipelines for Microsoft Teams integration to function. This is more about how access is granted based on conditions, not if the application can connect.

D. SSH authentication

This option is incorrect. SSH (Secure Shell) authentication is primarily used for secure shell access and Git operations (e.g., cloning repositories, pushing code) when using SSH keys instead of HTTPS with personal access tokens. It has no relevance to the Azure Pipelines integration with Microsoft Teams for notifications.

————————————————————————————————————————————————————

Correct Answer(s): Third-party application access via OAth

Third-party application access via OAuth is the CORRECT answer because we have a requirement to connect the azure pipelines and Microsoft teams. Since Azure Pipelines app uses the OAuth based authentication, in order to connect both Teams and Azure pipelines app, we need Third-party application access via OAuth for the organization to be enabled from the Security policies section in Azure DevOps Organization settings.

Documentation for integrating Azure Pipelines with Microsoft Teams:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/integrations/microsoft-teams

Alternate authentication credentials is an INCORRECT answer because this authentication method is not supported in the process of integrating Microsoft teams with the application of the Azure pipeline. Moreover, this authentication method is no longer supported by Azure DevOps.

SSH authentication is an INCORRECT answer because this option is enabled when we want to securely allow access for our repos by MacOS and Linux based devices. It won’t affect the process of MS teams and azure pipelines integration.

Azure Active Directory Conditional Access Policy Validation is an INCORRECT answer because this option is used when we want to restrict our Azure DevOps Organization’s access from outside or use MFA for the sign-in process. This option has nothing to do with the integration of Teams and pipelines.

question_html:
As part of your application build process, you need to deploy a group of resources to Azure by using an Azure Resource Manager template located on GitHub.
Which three actions should you perform in sequence?

1. Create a release pipeline.
2. Set the template parameters.
3. Add an Azure Resource Group Deployment task.
4. Create a package.
5. Create a job agent.
explanation_html:
Correct Answer(s): 1-3-2

  1. (1) Create a release pipeline: This is the starting point for defining the deployment process. A release pipeline in Azure DevOps allows you to automate the deployment steps for your application.

Within this task, you can define the location of your ARM template on GitHub (using a URL) and set any necessary parameters for the template.

  3. (2) Set the template parameters: The ARM template might require specific parameters to define things like resource names, locations, or sizes. In the Azure Resource Group Deployment task, you can configure these parameters with their corresponding values.

Here’s why the other actions are not part of the ideal sequence:

  • Create a package (Action 4): This isn’t necessary for deploying resources with an ARM template. The ARM template itself defines the resources to be deployed.
  • Create a job agent (Action 5): Job agents are used to run tasks in a specific environment. While you might need a job agent for your pipeline execution, creating it isn’t directly related to deploying resources with an ARM template. The pipeline itself can determine the appropriate agent based on your configuration.

question_html:
A company is planning on deploying an application to Azure. The web app will be deployed using the Azure Web App service. Azure Devops services will be used to manage the CI/CD process for the application. The company wants to implement blue green deployments for the web application.
Which of the following is the ideal service to use for blue green deployments?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option A. Azure Traffic Manager Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based traffic routing service that allows you to direct user requests to different endpoints. In a blue‑green deployment, you maintain two environments (blue = current, green = new). Traffic Manager makes it easy to switch traffic between these environments with minimal downtime, making it the ideal choice for blue‑green deployments in Azure Web Apps.

Incorrect

Option B. Azure Load Balancer Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and is used to distribute traffic across VMs in a single region. It does not provide DNS‑based routing between deployment slots or environments, so it is not suitable for blue‑green deployments of web apps.

Option C. Azure Application Gateway Azure Application Gateway is a Layer 7 load balancer with features like SSL termination, WAF, and URL‑based routing. While powerful for web traffic management, it is not the standard service for blue‑green deployments in Azure Web Apps. It is more suited for complex routing and security scenarios.

Option D. Azure Virtual Gateway Azure Virtual Network Gateway is used for VPN and ExpressRoute connections to enable secure connectivity between on‑premises and Azure networks. It has nothing to do with traffic routing for blue‑green deployments, making it incorrect in this context.

question_html:
The lead developer at your company reports that adding new application features takes longer than expected due to a large accumulated technical debt.
You need to recommend changes to reduce the accumulated technical debt.
Solution: You recommend increasing the test coverage.
Does this meet the goal?
explanation_html:
No

Explanation:

While increasing test coverage is a crucial part of software development best practices, it doesn’t directly address the root cause of accumulated technical debt.

  • Technical Debt refers to shortcuts or suboptimal design decisions made during development for faster delivery. These can include:

    • Poorly written code: Difficult to understand, maintain, and extend.
    • Insufficient documentation: Making it hard to understand how the system works.
    • Tightly coupled components: Making changes in one area difficult without impacting others.
    • Lack of modularity: Hindering code reusability and making it hard to isolate and fix issues.

  • Increased Test Coverage helps:

    • Identify regressions: Ensure that new changes don’t break existing functionality.
    • Improve code quality: By forcing developers to write more robust and maintainable code.

However, it doesn’t directly:

  • Refactor existing code: To improve its design, structure, and maintainability.
  • Address the root causes of the technical debt: Such as time pressures, lack of planning, or insufficient knowledge.

To effectively reduce technical debt, you should also consider:

  • Regular code reviews: To identify and address potential issues early on.
  • Dedicated refactoring sprints: To address specific areas of technical debt.
  • Investing in code quality tools: Such as static analysis tools and linters.
  • Improving development processes: To encourage better design and reduce the need for shortcuts.
  • Educating developers: On best practices, design patterns, and the importance of avoiding technical debt.

In summary:

Increasing test coverage is a valuable practice but not a sufficient solution for reducing accumulated technical debt. It needs to be part of a broader strategy that addresses the underlying issues and actively improves the codebase.
