Your team is planning on hosting a git repository using Azure repos. The team would be hosting the following types of files
– ASP.Net core code files
– Images, JavaScript files linked to the projects
The team wants to follow the best practices when it comes to hosting the files in a git-based repository.
Which of the following can be used to manage source files that large differences between versions and frequent updates to the files?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option C. Git LFS (Large File Storage)

  • Why correct:
    • Git LFS is designed to handle large binary files (e.g., images, media, graphics) that don’t compress well and often change significantly between versions.
    • Instead of storing the entire file in the Git history, Git LFS stores a pointer in the repository and keeps the actual file in a separate storage system.
    • This reduces repository size, improves performance, and ensures efficient version control for large files.
    • Best practice in Azure Repos (and Git in general) is to use Git LFS for large, frequently updated files.

Incorrect

Option A. Git locking

  • Git locking prevents multiple users from editing the same file simultaneously.
  • Useful for binary files that cannot be merged, but it does not solve the problem of large differences between versions.
  • More about concurrency control than storage optimization.

Option B. Git merge

  • Git merge is a standard operation to combine branches.
  • It does not address large file handling or storage efficiency.
  • Irrelevant to the problem of managing large binary files.

Option D. Git squash merge

  • Squash merge condenses multiple commits into a single commit for cleaner history.
  • While useful for commit management, it does not solve issues with large files or frequent updates.
  • Misleading distractor focusing on commit history rather than file storage.

explanation_html:
To create an alert specifically for an authentication error on the server, you need to filter the Application Insights log query based on a property that indicates the HTTP status code returned by the server.

  • B. resultCode: In Application Insights, the resultCode property (often found in requests or dependencies tables) typically stores the HTTP status code of a request. Authentication errors on a server are commonly indicated by HTTP status codes like 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden. Filtering on resultCode and specifying these error codes would allow you to capture authentication failures. The exhibit shows resultCode as a filterable facet on the left, indicating it’s a key attribute for requests.

Incorrect:

  • A. itemType: This property indicates the type of telemetry item (e.g., request, dependency, exception, trace, pageView). While it’s useful for broad filtering, it does not provide granular detail about the nature of an error like an authentication failure. You would likely filter on itemType == "request" first, but then need a further filter.
  • C. source: This property generally refers to the origin of the telemetry (e.g., the application name or instance). It doesn’t provide information about the specific type of error that occurred.
  • D. success: The success property is a boolean (true or false) that indicates whether a request or dependency call was successful. While success == false would tell you that some error occurred, it doesn’t specifically pinpoint an authentication error. Many types of errors (e.g., server errors like 500s, client errors like 404s) would result in success == false. To isolate authentication errors, you need the specific resultCode.

2. Create a Microsoft Visual Studio project that includes all the packages.
3. Create a NuGet package.
4. Run an initial package restore.
5. Modify the configuration files to reference the Azure Artifacts feed.
6. Create an npm package.
explanation_html:
The three actions you should perform in sequence to consolidate packages into a single, reliable Azure Artifacts feed are: 1-5-4

  1. (1) Create an Azure Artifacts feed that uses upstream sources: This is the foundation for consolidating packages. The Azure Artifacts feed acts as a central repository that retrieves packages from the unreliable public feeds.
  2. (5) Modify configuration files to reference the feed: Update your project’s configuration files to point to the newly created Azure Artifacts feed instead of the public feeds. This ensures your project downloads packages from your reliable internal source.
  3. (4) Run an initial package restore: After creating the feed and updating configurations, run a package restore to populate your Azure Artifacts feed with all the necessary packages.

These steps effectively consolidate packages and improve your project’s build and deployment stability by eliminating reliance on unreliable public feeds.

question_html:
You use Azure DevOps to manage the build and deployment of an app named App1.
You have a release pipeline that deploys a virtual machine named VM1.
You plan to monitor the release pipeline by using Azure Monitor.
You need to create an alert to monitor the performance of VM1. The alert must be triggered when the average CPU usage exceeds 70 percent for five minutes. The alert must calculate the average once every minute.
You need to configure the alert for the Aggregation granularity (Period).
What should you choose?
explanation_html:
The correct option is A. 1 minute.

When configuring an Azure Monitor alert, the Aggregation granularity (Period) specifies how often the metric data is collected and aggregated before being evaluated against the alert rule’s threshold.

In this scenario:

  • The requirement is to “calculate the average once every minute.” This directly translates to the Aggregation granularity (Period).
  • The alert needs to be triggered “when the average CPU usage exceeds 70 percent for five minutes.” This “five minutes” refers to the Frequency of evaluation or Threshold duration, meaning the condition must persist for five consecutive 1-minute periods before the alert fires. It does not mean the aggregation period itself is five minutes.

Choosing “1 minute” for the Aggregation granularity allows Azure Monitor to sample and average the CPU usage every minute. These 1-minute averages are then used by the alert rule to determine if the 70% threshold has been continuously exceeded for the specified five-minute duration.

Incorrect:

  • B. 3 minute: Choosing 3 minutes would mean the CPU usage is averaged over 3-minute intervals. This would not meet the requirement to calculate the average “once every minute.”
  • C. 5 minute: If the Aggregation granularity were 5 minutes, the alert would only evaluate the average CPU usage over a 5-minute block. This would not allow for the “for five minutes” condition to be accurately met based on 1-minute averages, as each data point would already represent a 5-minute average.
  • D. 7 minute: Similar to 3 and 5 minutes, a 7-minute aggregation granularity would not fulfill the requirement of calculating the average every minute.

question_html: You intend to make use of Azure Artifacts to share packages that you wrote, tested, validated, and deployed. You want to use a solitary feed to release several builds of each package. You have to make sure that the release of packages that are in development is restricted. Which of the following actions should you take?

options.text: You should make use of dynamic code analysis.
You should make use of static code analysis.
You should make use of views.
You should make use of upstream sources.

explanation_html:
Correct:
C. You should make use of views.
Feed Views allow you to filter the packages available to consumers. A common pattern is to have a @Local view for all builds and a @Release view for validated builds. By promoting only “validated and deployed“ packages to a specific view (like a “Release“ view), you ensure that consumers (like developers or production pipelines) only see the stable versions. This effectively restricts access to “in-development“ packages without needing multiple separate feeds.

Incorrect:
A & B. Dynamic and Static code analysis.
DAST and SAST are security testing methodologies used during the build or run phase of a pipeline to find vulnerabilities in code. While they help “validate“ a package, they are not mechanisms for controlling the visibility or sharing of packages within an Artifacts feed.

E. You should make use of upstream sources.
Upstream sources are used to bring in packages from external feeds (like NuGet.org, npmjs.com, or other Azure DevOps feeds) into your local feed. They do not provide a mechanism to restrict the release or visibility of your own internal development builds within a single feed.

?You have a GitHub private repository for a library used by your organization. This repository is integrated with an Azure Boards project which is used to manage the project backlog. You adopt a pull request and commit guidelines to automatically generate release notes. Every two weeks you create a new git tag for this library following semantic versioning.
You need to define the best place to communicate with the library users regarding the changes in a specific version of the library.
Where should you store the release notes?
explanation_html:
You should store the release notes with GitHub releases. This makes it easy for the library users to see the changes in a specific version that is published with the git tags. In GitHub releases, alongside the release notes and the corresponding git tag, you can include links to binary files and source code packages.
You should not store the release notes with the work item acceptance criteria. The acceptance criteria field in a work item should describe what is expected in order for a work item to be considered as complete.
You should not store the release notes with the work item or pull requests description. You can use these fields to describe what a specific feature does and give more details about it. This is not the best place to store the release notes because a two-week release might include multiple features, compelling the library users to spend a lot of time to be able to understand what is new. Instead you can include a link to pull requests or work items in your release notes in order to allow the library users to understand the features in more detail.

question_html:
A company has several IT development departments. The departments are constantly working on new features.
You need to specify which branches should trigger a continuous integration pipeline when new code is pushed. The pipeline should run even if the branch does not have an open pull request.
Which action should you perform to accomplish this task?

options.text: Create a pull request (PR) trigger and specify which branches should be processed.
Create a release trigger and specify which branches should be processed.
Create a continuous integration (CI) trigger and specify which branches should be processed.
Create a scheduled trigger that contains only feature branches and set this trigger to run every hour.

explanation_html:
You should create a continuous integration (CI) trigger and specify which branches should be processed. This allows you to specify which branch or branches trigger a pipeline run when new code is pushed.
You should not create a pull request (PR) trigger and specify which branches should be processed. This would allow a pipeline to run whenever a pull request is opened with one of the specified target branches, or when changes are pushed to such a pull request. This would not trigger a pipeline run from branches without a pull request open.
You should not create a scheduled trigger that contains only feature branches and set this trigger to run every hour. This would allow a pipeline to be triggered for specific branches based on a schedule. This would not trigger a pipeline when new code is pushed to a branch.
You should not create a release trigger and specify which branches should be processed. This would allow you to trigger a continuous deployment pipeline that deploys the application to production environments.

question_html: Which of the following choices is the exact number of days of history you can import Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC) to Git using the “Import repository“ feature in Azure DevOps?

options.text: There are some limitations here (that apply only when migrating source type TFVC) to a single branch and only 180 days of history

explanation_html:
Correct:
B. 180 days
The native “Import repository“ tool in Azure DevOps is designed for a simplified migration. It has a hard-coded limit where it can only import up to the last 180 days of history. This limit exists to ensure the migration process remains performant and doesn‘t time out or create an excessively bloated Git repository during the conversion process.

Incorrect:
A. 90 days
This is incorrect. While many Azure DevOps retention policies (like build or release logs) default to 30 or 90 days, the TFVC import limit is specifically set at 180 days.

C. 365 days
This is incorrect. One year of history exceeds the capability of the web-based “Import repository“ tool. To migrate a full year of history (or more), an administrator would need to use external tools like Git-TFS.

D. There are some limitations here…
While this statement contains factual information (referencing the 180-day limit and the single-branch restriction), in the context of a multiple-choice exam, it is a distractor. The question asks for the “exact number of days,“ making Option B the direct and correct answer.

question_html:
A company is planning on Azure DevOps. They want to use DevOps practices for the development and deployment of applications. They have the following patterns. They want to implement different development teams when it comes to Build automation.
-Ensure that only code that compiles and passes unit testing is checked into the Integration branch.
-Ensure that code is of good quality before it is released to the test area.
-Ensure that security vulnerabilities are identified as soon as possible in the code base.
Which of the following technique in build automation can be used for the following requirement?
Ensure that only code that compiles and passes unit testing is checked into the Integration branch.
explanation_html:
The technique in build automation that can be used for the requirement “Ensure that only code that compiles and passes unit testing is checked into the Integration branch“ is Gated Check-ins.
Gated Check-ins is a build automation technique that requires code changes to pass certain conditions, such as code compilation and unit tests, before they can be checked into the main branch or integration branch. This ensures that any code changes that are checked in meet a minimum quality standard and do not break the build.
Gated Check-ins can be implemented using Azure DevOps build pipelines, where the build process is triggered automatically when code is checked in. If the code changes fail to pass the specified conditions, the build process fails, and the code changes are not checked in.
By implementing Gated Check-ins, development teams can ensure that only high-quality code changes are integrated into the main codebase, reducing the risk of introducing defects into the codebase and improving overall code quality.
Therefore, in this scenario, the appropriate technique in build automation that can be used for the requirement “Ensure that only code that compiles and passes unit testing is checked into the Integration branch“ is Gated Check-ins.

A company is planning on Azure DevOps. They want to use DevOps practices for the development and deployment of applications. They have the following patterns. They want to implement different development teams when it comes to Build automation.

Which of the following technique in build automation can be used for the following requirement?
Ensure that security vulnerabilities are identified as soon as possible in the code base.
explanation_html:
The technique in build automation that can be used for the requirement “Ensure that security vulnerabilities are identified as soon as possible in the code base“ is Code Analysis Integrations.
Code analysis is a technique that allows developers to identify security vulnerabilities, performance issues, and other potential problems in code before it is compiled or executed. Code analysis tools can be integrated into the build process to automatically scan code for issues and provide feedback to developers.
By integrating code analysis into the build process, developers can identify and address security vulnerabilities early in the development process, reducing the risk of introducing security issues into the codebase. This approach also helps to ensure that security standards are met consistently, reducing the time and effort required to address security issues later in the development process.
There are several code analysis tools available for Azure DevOps, including SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Veracode. These tools can be integrated into the build process using Azure DevOps tasks or plugins, allowing developers to run code analysis scans automatically during the build process.
Therefore, in this scenario, the appropriate technique in build automation that can be used for the requirement “Ensure that security vulnerabilities are identified as soon as possible in the code base“ is Code Analysis Integrations.

The lead developer at your company reports that adding new application features takes longer than expected due to a large accumulated technical debt.
You need to recommend changes to reduce the accumulated technical debt.
Solution: You recommend reducing the code coupling and the dependency cycles?
Does this meet the goal?
explanation_html:
Reducing code coupling and dependency cycles can certainly help reduce technical debt. Code coupling refers to the degree to which one module or component depends on another. High coupling can make the code more difficult to understand, test, and maintain, leading to an increase in technical debt. By reducing code coupling, you can make the code more modular and easier to work with, which can help reduce technical debt.
Dependency cycles occur when two or more modules depend on each other in a circular manner. This can make it difficult to understand, test, and maintain the code, leading to an increase in technical debt. By breaking dependency cycles, you can make the code more modular and easier to work with, which can help reduce technical debt.
However, there are also other methods that can be used to reduce technical debt. For example, some best practices for reducing technical debt include acknowledging tech debt, classifying and documenting tech debt, understanding your technology adoption stage and identifying the best approach to avoid technical debt, selecting a scalable app architecture, making code review a routine, keeping a record of changes, and educating non-technical stakeholders1. Its important to take a comprehensive approach to reducing technical debt that addresses its underlying causes. So yes, your recommendation meets the goal but there are also other methods that can be used in conjunction with your recommendation.

? Consolidate commit histories.
? Merge the changes into a single commit.
Which merge strategy should you use in the branch policy?
explanation_html:
Squash merging is a merge option that allows you to condense the Git history of topic branches when you complete a pull request. Instead of each commit on the topic branch being added to the history of the default branch, a squash merge takes all the file changes and adds them to a single new commit on the default branch.
A simple way to think about this is that squash merge gives you just the file changes, and a regular merge gives you the file changes and the commit history.
Note: Squash merging keeps your default branch histories clean and easy to follow without demanding any workflow changes on your team. Contributors to the topic branch work how they want in the topic branch, and the default branches keep a linear history through the use of squash merges. The commit history of a master branch updated with squash merges will have one commit for each merged branch. You can step through this history commit by commit to find out exactly when work was done.
References:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/merging-with-squash

You need to implement static code analysis.
During which phase should you use static code analysis?
explanation_html:
Build
Static code analysis should be implemented during the build phase of the software development lifecycle.
Static code analysis is a technique that helps developers identify potential defects and security vulnerabilities in code before it is compiled or executed. This analysis can be automated using tools that analyze the source code and flag potential issues such as syntax errors, security vulnerabilities, and code smells.
By incorporating static code analysis into the build process, developers can detect and fix issues early in the development process, reducing the risk of introducing defects into the codebase. This approach also helps to ensure that code quality standards are met consistently, even under time pressure.
While it is possible to perform static code analysis during other phases of the software development lifecycle such as integration testing, staging, or production release, it is most effective when performed during the build phase. This allows issues to be detected and addressed as early as possible, reducing the time and effort required to fix defects later in the development process.
Therefore, in this scenario, static code analysis should be implemented during the build phase of the software development lifecycle.

Quality validation. Query metrics from tests on the build artifacts such as pass rate or code coverage and deploy only if they are within required thresholds.

This ensures that you are meeting the key health/performance metrics (KPIs) as your applications move from dev to production and any differences in the infrastructure environment or scale is not negatively impacting your KPIs.

Typically, gates are used in connection with incident management, problem management, change management, monitoring, and external approval systems.

question_html:
You are building an ASP.NET Core application.
You plan to create an application utilization baseline by capturing telemetry data.
You need to add code to the application to capture the telemetry data. The solution must minimize the costs of storing the telemetry data.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Add the <initialsamplingpercentage>99</initialsamplingpercentage> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.
From the code of the application, enable adaptive sampling.
From the code of the application, add Azure Application Insights telemetry.
Add the <maxtelemetryitemspersecond>5</maxtelemetryitemspersecond> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.
From the code of the application, disable adaptive sampling.

explanation_html:
Sampling is a feature in Azure Application Insights. It is the recommended way to reduce telemetry traffic, data costs, and storage costs, while preserving a statistically correct analysis of application data.
The Application Insights SDK for ASP.NET Core supports both fixed-rate and adaptive sampling. Adaptive sampling is enabled by default.
D: For adaptive sampling: The volume is adjusted automatically to keep within a specified maximum rate of traffic, and is controlled via the setting
MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond. If the application produces a low amount of telemetry, such as when debugging or due to low usage, items won‘t be dropped by the sampling processor as long as volume is below MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond.
Note: In ApplicationInsights.config, you can adjust several parameters in the AdaptiveSamplingTelemetryProcessor node. The figures shown are the default values:
5
Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/sampling

You are making use of Azure DevOps to automate the build process for a Java-based application.

explanation_html:
JaCoCo is a free and open-source code coverage tool for Java. It can be used to measure the percentage of code that is executed by your tests. JaCoCo can be integrated with Azure DevOps to automatically publish code coverage results to the pipeline.
Cobertura is another free and open-source code coverage tool for Java. It is similar to JaCoCo, but it does not support integration with Azure DevOps.
Coverage.py is a Python tool that can be used to measure code coverage for Python applications. It cannot be integrated with Azure DevOps.
Here are some additional details about JaCoCo and Cobertura:
JaCoCo is a more popular tool than Cobertura. It is used by many large companies, including Google, Amazon, and Netflix.
JaCoCo provides more detailed code coverage reports than Cobertura. It can also measure branch coverage, which is not possible with Cobertura.
JaCoCo is easier to integrate with Azure DevOps than Cobertura. There is a dedicated task in Azure DevOps for publishing JaCoCo code coverage results.
References: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/test/publish-code-coverage-results

question_html:
You are in the process of creating a new Java application.
You analyze the code of .NET applications via a SonarQube server.
You are preparing to add a task type to the build pipeline that will allow you to analyze and monitor the code quality of the Java application.
Which two of the following task types could you use?
explanation_html: SonarQube is a set of static analyzers that can be used to identify areas of improvement in your code. It allows you to analyze the technical debt in your project and keep track of it in the future. With Maven and Gradle build tasks, you can run SonarQube analysis with minimal setup in a new or existing Azure DevOps Services build task. Reference: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/java/sonarqube?view=azure-devops

question_html: Which work item type can be used in a Kanban board to represent expedited work in an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) project in Azure DevOps?
explanation_html: An impediment work item type can be used to represent expedited work in a Kanban board for an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) project in Azure DevOps. Impediments typically indicate that there are urgent or high-priority issues that need immediate attention and resolution, and are often used to address blockers or critical situations affecting the flow of work.

question_html: Your organization uses Azure DevOps and Microsoft Teams. You are working as a release pipeline engineer. Due to compliance requirements, you need to request approval from users that are not connected to the Azure DevOps organization before the release pipeline is started. What can you configure to achieve the goal?

options.text: Configure a custom approval policy in Azure DevOps.
Create a manual intervention task in the release pipeline.
Configure a webhook trigger to send a notification to Microsoft Teams.
Use an Azure Logic App to send an approval request to Microsoft Teams.

explanation_html: Azure Logic Apps can be used to create custom workflows that integrate with various services, including Microsoft Teams. By using an Azure Logic App, you can design a workflow that sends an approval request to users in Microsoft Teams who are not connected to the Azure DevOps organization. Once the users approve or reject the request, the Logic App can then communicate the response back to the release pipeline, either allowing it to proceed or stopping it based on the approval status. This approach enables you to meet the compliance requirements by involving external users in the release pipeline approval process.

question_html:
Scenario

You are creating a multi-stage Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core 2.2 application. You have the following partially completed code:

Dockerfile

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/sdk:2.2 AS build-env
WORKDIR /app

# Copy csproj and restore as distinct layers
COPY *.csproj ./
RUN dotnet restore

# Copy everything else and build
COPY . ./
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o out

# Build runtime image
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/aspnet:2.2
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build-env /app/out .

[SLOT4] ["dotnet", "PROJECT_NAME.dll"]

Question

Which of the following should replace [SLOT4] to ensure the container correctly executes the application upon startup?
explanation_html:
The correct answer is

C (ENTRYPOINT).

In Docker, the ENTRYPOINT instruction is used to define the primary executable that should run when a container starts. Once defined, the container acts as if it were an executable file. By using the exec form ["executable", "param1", "param2"], you ensure that the application receives Unix signals (like SIGTERM) properly, which is critical for graceful shutdowns in orchestrated environments like Kubernetes.

Why the others are incorrect:

  • A & B: These are base image references used with the FROM instruction to define the environment. They are not executable commands.

  • D (RUN): The RUN instruction executes commands during the build process (to create the layers of the image). It is not meant for starting the application when the container launches.

  • E (FROM): This is used to initialize a new build stage. Putting this in the final line would attempt to start a new, redundant stage instead of defining how to run the app.

Best Practices in Multi-Stage Builds

The provided Dockerfile follows a standard pattern for optimizing image size:

  • Build Stage: Uses the large SDK image containing compilers and tools.

  • Runtime Stage: Uses the lightweight aspnet image. By copying only the published output (/app/out) from the build stage, you create a production-ready image that is significantly smaller and more secure, as it does not contain the source code or build tools.

question_html:
Your company has a Git repository hosted in Azure DevOps. You have to configure the pull requests in a branch to meet the following requirements before they are merged:

  • Ensure that the committed code is compiled successfully.

  • Ensure that pull requests have a Quality gate status of passed in SonarCloud.

Which of the following must be configured in the branch policy settings to satisfy these requirements?
explanation_html:
The correct answer is A (A build policy).

  1. Build Validation (Build Policy): In Azure DevOps, you configure Build Validation policies to ensure that code changes don’t break the build and meet quality standards. When you integrate SonarCloud, you typically trigger a CI pipeline that runs the analysis. This pipeline must pass for the build policy to be satisfied.

  2. How SonarCloud interacts: SonarCloud publishes a “status” to the PR. If you have configured the SonarCloud extension correctly, the build pipeline will fail if the Quality Gate is not met. Therefore, the Build Policy acts as the gatekeeper, failing the build (and thus the policy) if the code does not meet the criteria.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Check-in policy: These are legacy features specific to Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC), not Git repositories in Azure DevOps.

  • C. Status policy: While you can manually add status checks, “Build Validation” is the standard, built-in mechanism for integrating CI/CD pipelines and external quality tools like SonarCloud into the branch protection workflow.

  • D. Deployment policy: This relates to Release Pipelines and environment gates, not the PR merge process in a Git repository.

Summary Table: Policy Types in Azure DevOps

Policy Feature Used For
Build Validation Ensures code compiles and automated tests (including quality gates) pass before merging.
Required Reviewers Ensures code is reviewed by specific team members or groups.
Comment Resolution Prevents merging until all comments on the PR are marked as resolved.
Work Item Linking Ensures every PR is associated with at least one work item (e.g., a User Story).

question_html:
Your team uses a Git repository in Azure DevOps. You want to merge feature branches into the main branch. Your team’s primary requirement is to preserve the full, non-linear history of all commits from the feature branch, including the explicit merge commit that indicates when the feature was integrated.

Which of the following merge types should you use?
explanation_html:
The Basic merge (no fast-forward)—often denoted in Git as --no-ff—is specifically designed to preserve the history of a feature branch as a distinct set of commits joined to the main line.

Breakdown of Merge Strategies:

  1. Basic merge (no-fast-forward) [Correct]: Even if the main branch hasn’t moved forward, Git creates a new “merge commit.” This creates a clear visual “loop” in your history graph, showing exactly where a feature branch started and ended. This is the gold standard for teams that need to see the exact context of when work was integrated.

  2. Rebase and fast-forward: This rewrites the commit history of the feature branch, placing the commits directly on top of the latest commit of the target branch. This results in a perfectly linear history, but it removes the information about when the branch was actually merged.

  3. Squash merge: This takes all the commits from the feature branch and condenses them into a single new commit on the target branch. This is excellent for keeping the main branch clean but discards the granular history of the feature development.

  4. Rebase with merge commit: This is less common in standard Git workflows. It typically rebases the feature branch first (making it linear) and then forces a merge commit. This is often redundant and can lead to confusing history if not managed correctly.

Summary Comparison

Merge Strategy History Style Preserves Individual Commits? Shows Merge Point?
No-Fast-Forward Non-Linear Yes Yes
Squash Linear No (Squashed into one) No
Fast-Forward Linear Yes No

question_html: In which of the following scenarios would you typically encounter the largest amount of accumulated technical debt?
explanation_html:
Correct Answer: B. Brownfield project

A Brownfield project refers to the development or deployment of new software or systems in an environment where existing systems, legacy code, or established infrastructure are already in place.

Why Brownfield projects contain the most technical debt:

  • Legacy Constraints: You are working with an existing, often older, codebase that may use outdated frameworks or patterns.
  • Accumulated Decisions: Over years of maintenance, previous teams may have made “quick fixes” or workarounds that were never refactored, leading to significant technical debt.
  • Integration Complexity: You often have to build new functionality that integrates with rigid, older systems, which forces compromises in architecture.

Contrast with other choices:

  • Greenfield projects: These involve building a system from scratch, often on a clean slate. While you can still write “bad code,” you are not starting with the “baggage” of inherited technical debt from years of previous development.
  • Proof of Concept (PoC): These are meant to be short-lived experiments to validate an idea. While they may have “intentional” technical debt (because the code is not meant for production), it is usually not the same scale as a large, multi-year legacy system.

question_html:
A team is planning on creating, testing, validating, and deploying packages by using Azure Artifacts. They need to ensure that multiple builds of each package can be released through specific lifecycle stages (e.g., Pre-release, Release) using a single feed.

Which of the following would be ideal for this scenario?
explanation_html:
Correct Answer: B. Views

Views allow you to create “virtual” subsets of your feed, which act as quality gates for your packages.

  1. Lifecycle Management: By default, every feed includes views like @Local, @Prerelease, and @Release. You can promote specific versions of a package from the @Local view (where it is first published) to the @Prerelease or @Release views once it has passed testing or validation.

  2. Controlled Consumption: Consumers can point their configuration files (like nuget.config or .npmrc) to a specific view (e.g., https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/.../my-feed@Release/nuget/v3/index.json). This ensures that only packages that have been promoted to that “Release” view are visible and available to production deployment pipelines, effectively filtering out unstable or under-development versions.

  3. Why others are incorrect:

    • Upstream Sources (A): As you noted, these are used for proxying and caching packages from external, remote sources. They do not help with promoting internal builds through different stages of a release.

    • Downstream sources (C): This is not a standard Azure Artifacts terminology or feature.

    • Local symbols (D): Symbol servers are used for debugging compiled code (like C++ or .NET PDBs), not for managing the release lifecycle of package versions.

Summary Table: Views vs. Upstream Sources

Feature Purpose Lifecycle Management?
Views Create filtered perspectives of a feed for promotion/release. Yes (Promotion model)
Upstream Sources Proxy external/public registry packages into your feed. No

question_html:
Your company has a Git repository hosted in Azure DevOps. You have to configure the pull requests in a branch to meet the following requirements before they are merged:

  • Ensure that the committed code is compiled successfully.

  • Ensure that pull requests have a Quality gate status of passed in SonarCloud.

Which of the following must be configured in the branch policy settings to satisfy the requirement: “Ensure that pull requests have a Quality gate status of passed in SonarCloud”?
explanation_html:
Correct Answer:

A. A build policy (Build Validation)

The ambiguity exists because the SonarCloud extension does register a “Status” in the Azure DevOps PR view, but to make that status a blocking requirement for merging, you must use the Build Validation branch policy.

  1. Build Validation (A): This policy triggers a CI pipeline. When you use the SonarCloud Azure DevOps extension, the SonarCloud analysis is part of this pipeline. If the Quality Gate fails, the build pipeline fails. Because the policy is set to “Required,” the Pull Request is blocked from merging. This is the official mechanism for enforcing automated quality checks in Git branch policies.

  2. Status Policy (C): In modern Azure DevOps, you can add a “Status Policy” to require specific statuses from external services. While this technically can work for Quality Gates, the exam board standardizes on Build Validation as the primary DevOps-native way to integrate CI pipelines and quality checks into the PR lifecycle.

  3. Check-in Policy (B): As noted, this is exclusive to the older TFVC (Team Foundation Version Control) and does not apply to modern Git repositories.

  4. Deployment Policy (D): This is irrelevant to the PR merge process, as deployment policies are concerned with release gates and environment promotions, not source code verification.

question_html:
Photonapps Overview

Photonapps is an online training provider that has established an Azure DevOps organization to modernize its development lifecycle.

Organizational Context

  • Infrastructure: A custom agent pool named photonapppool containing 5 Windows Server 2016 virtual machines.

  • Tools: Includes a Docker extension for containerized workflows.

Projects & Requirements

Project Objective Key Requirement
photonappA Incremental builds Support for optimizing build times through incremental processing.
photonappB Quality integration Integration with SonarQube for static code analysis.
photonappC Containerization Build pipeline creating a Docker image for Azure Container Registry (ACR).
photonappD Git triggers Trigger a build on commits, but exclude the /data folder.
photonappE Desired state Use Azure Automation State Configuration for photonappgroup.
photonappF Quality gates Deployment pipelines that require 0 active bugs.

Question: photonappD Configuration

You need to comply with the requirement for the project “photonappD” to prevent pipeline triggers when changes occur within the /data folder. Which of the following would you set?

options.text: A. A branch filter to exclude
B. A branch filter to include
C. A path filter to include
D. A path filter to exclude

explanation_html:
Correct Answer: D. A path filter to exclude

  • Correct Choice (D): To ensure the pipeline does not trigger when files in /data are modified, you must configure a path filter to exclude. In Azure Pipelines YAML, this is done by adding the folder to the exclude section of your trigger settings (e.g., paths: exclude: - /data/**).

  • Incorrect Choice (A & B): Branch filters are used to restrict triggers to specific branches (like main or release/*). They control which branch updates trigger a build, not which files within those branches trigger it.

  • Incorrect Choice (C): A path filter to include would restrict the build to trigger only when changes occur within the specified path, which is the exact opposite of the requirement to ignore the /data directory.

question_html:
You use Azure SQL Database Intelligent Insights and Azure Application Insights for monitoring.

You need to write ad-hoc queries against the monitoring data collected in your Log Analytics workspace.

Which query language should you use?
explanation_html:
Correct Answer:

A. Kusto Query Language (KQL)

  1. Kusto Query Language (KQL): This is the native query language for Azure Monitor logs and Application Insights. It is designed to be highly efficient for log analysis, time-series data, and large-scale data exploration.

  2. Transact-SQL (T-SQL): While T-SQL is used for querying Azure SQL Databases (relational data), it is not used to query Application Insights telemetry or Log Analytics workspace logs.

  3. PL/pgSQL and PL/SQL: These are procedural languages used for PostgreSQL and Oracle databases, respectively, and have no role in querying Azure monitoring telemetry.

Sometimes, exams will list the platform (e.g., “Log Analytics”) as an option because they are poorly phrased. However, KQL is the specific language you must know for the AZ-400 certification when dealing with log-based monitoring data in Azure.

question_html:
Your company uses Azure DevOps for managing source control and pipelines. You have a Git repository and need to implement a pull request merge strategy that minimizes the number of commits and reduces the overall volume of the history in the main branch.

You decide to implement a pull request strategy that uses fast-forward merges.

Does this fulfill your requirement to reduce the history volume?
explanation_html:
No

Because a fast-forward merge simply adopts the existing commit history of the feature branch and places it into the main branch. If your feature branch has 20 small “work-in-progress” commits, all 20 of those commits will be added to the main branch history.

Why the alternatives differ:

  1. Fast-Forward / Standard Merges: These preserve the granularity of your work. While they might be linear, they do not “reduce” the volume of the history—they retain every individual commit made during development.

  2. Squash Merge (The correct way to reduce volume): This takes all commits from a feature branch and “squashes” them into a single new commit on the main branch. This is the primary strategy for teams that want to keep a clean, concise main branch history without the clutter of granular, intermediate development commits.

Note:

In an Azure DevOps environment, you configure these strategies under Project Settings > Repositories > Policies > Branch Policies. Choosing the right strategy is a balance between:

  • Traceability: Keeping every commit (Standard Merge / Fast-Forward).

  • Cleanliness: Keeping the main branch easy to read (Squash Merge).

question_html:
Your team has code hosted in a GitHub repository. You need to connect an Azure Boards project with this GitHub.com repository.

Which of the following roles must the user possess on the GitHub repository to successfully establish the connection?

(Choose two valid answers; each is a complete solution.)
explanation_html:
Correct Answers: A and B

To connect Azure Boards to GitHub, the integration requires authorization that can modify repository webhooks and manage services. Only users with high-level access have the authority to perform these actions.

  • Administrator (A) & Owner (B): These roles have the necessary permissions to manage repository settings, including the configuration of Webhooks and Services, which are the fundamental mechanisms GitHub uses to “talk” to Azure Boards.

  • Why Reader (C) is incorrect: A “Reader” has read-only access to the code. They lack the administrative rights required to create integration webhooks or authorize third-party OAuth applications, which is essential for the handshake between GitHub and Azure DevOps.

  • Why Default (D) is incorrect: This is not a standard GitHub repository role.

Important Prerequisite Clarification

For the connection to work, the user must satisfy requirements on both sides of the connection:

  1. In Azure DevOps/Boards: The user must be a member of the Project Administrators group.

  2. In GitHub: The user must be an Owner or Administrator of the specific repository (or the organization) being connected.

This “dual-authentication” check ensures that only someone with governance authority in both systems can link them, preventing unauthorized integrations.
